questions.html: In a direct-mapped cache, how are the different bits of the memory address used? (Select all correct options.)

options.html: The tag bits are used to uniquely identify which block of main memory is currently stored in a cache line.
The index bits are used to select which cache line a memory block maps to.
The byte offset bits are used to select the specific byte within a cache block.
The tag bits are used to select which cache line a memory block maps to.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

The tag bits are always used to uniquely identify which block of main memory is currently stored in a cache line.

In a direct-mapped cache, the index bits are used to select which cache line a memory block maps to. (For a set associative cache, the index bits are used to select which cache set a memory block maps to. & for a fully associative cache, there are no index bits.)

The byte offset bits are always used to select the specific byte within a cache block.

questions.html:
Assume a system with:

  • $8$-bit memory addresses
     
  • direct-mapped cache
     
  • $2$-byte cache block size
     
  • $4$ cache lines

Which of the following pairs of memory addresses belong to different memory blocks but map to the same cache line? (Addresses are specified in base-$2$.)
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Number of byte offset bits = 1

Number of index bits = 2

Number of tag bits = 5

Address format = [tag (5 bits)][index (2 bits)][offset (1 bit)]

Method:

Breakdown each 8-bit address into [tag (5) | index (2) | offset (1)])


NOTE that two memory addresses belong to the same block if and only if they have the same index \& same tag.

Different blocks but same line $\rightarrow$ same index, different tag.

  1. $00000000 \rightarrow \operatorname{tag}=00000$, index $=00$, offset $=0$
    $00001000 \rightarrow$ tag=00001, index=00, offset=0

    $\rightarrow$ same index (00) but different tags $\rightarrow$ different blocks mapping to the same line.

  2. $00100101 \rightarrow \operatorname{tag}=00100$, index $=10$, offset $=1$
    $01100101 \rightarrow$ tag $=01100$, index $=10$, offset $=1$

    $\rightarrow$ same index (10) but different tags $\rightarrow$ different blocks mapping to the same line.

  3. $01010010 \rightarrow$ tag=01010, index=01, offset=0
    $01010011 \rightarrow$ tag $=01010$, index $=01$, offset $=1$


    $\rightarrow$ same index (01) and same tags $\rightarrow$ same blocks (mapping to same line, obviously)

    $01101010$

  4. $01101010 \rightarrow$ tag=01101, index=01, offset=0
    $01101100 \rightarrow$ tag=01101, index=10, offset=0

    $\rightarrow$ different index $\rightarrow$ different blocks mapping to different lines.

7. R$00000000$

Each operation above is either a hit or a miss, which indicates whether the data is found in the cache or not. All cache lines are initially empty. When a block is evicted, select the victim using the LRU (Least Recently Used) replacement policy.

What is the total number of cache misses that occur during this sequence?

Number of index bits = 2

2. W$00011011$ - Hit

3. R$11111000$-Compulsory Miss, Maps to set 0

5. R$01101000$ - Compulsory Miss, Maps to set 0

6. W$00001001$ - Compulsory Miss, Maps to set 0, Tag 11111 evicted

Based on the system specifications provided in the image, here is the detailed step-by-step solution.

 

1. System Configuration & Address Breakdown

 

First, we must determine how the 8-bit memory address is interpreted by the cache hardware.

  • Block Offset:

    • Block Size = 2 bytes = $2^1$ bytes.

    • Offset = 1 bit (The Least Significant Bit).

  • Set Index:

    • Number of Sets = 4 = $2^2$.

    • Set Index = 2 bits (The bits immediately to the left of the offset).

  • Tag:

    • Remaining bits = $8 \text{ (total)} - 2 \text{ (set)} - 1 \text{ (offset)} = \mathbf{5 \text{ bits}}$.

Address Format: [ Tag (5 bits) ] [ Set (2 bits) ] [ Offset (1 bit) ]

 

2. Operation Trace Table

 

We will track the state of the relevant sets (Set 0 and Set 1) for each operation.

  • Associativity: 2-way (Maximum 2 blocks per set).

  • Replacement: LRU (Least Recently Used). The set state is shown as {MRU, LRU} (Most Recently Used first).

questions.html: Consider a system with a block size of $p$ words. What is the range of words present in the $\mathrm{k^{th}}$ block of main memory?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

The correct answer is A. $k \cdot p \text{ to } (k+1) \cdot p - 1$.

Here is the step-by-step derivation:

 

1. Understanding Block Organization

 

Main memory is essentially a long list of words addressed linearly: $0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$

This memory is divided into fixed-size chunks called blocks.

  • Block Size ($p$): This means every block holds exactly $p$ words.

  • Block Index ($k$): We assume standard 0-based indexing where the first block is Block 0, the second is Block 1, and so on.

 

2. Deriving the Start Address

 

To find the starting word of Block $k$, we just need to count how many words are contained in all the blocks that come before it.

  • Before Block $k$, there are exactly $k$ blocks (Block $0$ to Block $k-1$).

  • Since each block has $p$ words, the total words before Block $k$ is $k \times p$.

  • Therefore, the first word of Block $k$ starts at address:

     

    $$\text{Start Address} = k \cdot p$$

 

3. Deriving the End Address

 

Since the block contains $p$ words, the addresses range from the start address to Start + p - 1.

  • $\text{End Address} = \text{Start Address} + (p - 1)$

  • $\text{End Address} = k \cdot p + p - 1$

  • Factoring out $p$, we get:

     

    $$\text{End Address} = (k + 1) \cdot p - 1$$

 

Example Verification

 

Let's assume the block size is 4 words ($p = 4$).

  • Block 0 ($k=0$): Contains words 0, 1, 2, 3.

    • Formula A: $0 \cdot 4$ to $(1) \cdot 4 - 1 \Rightarrow 0 \text{ to } 3$. (Correct)

  • Block 1 ($k=1$): Contains words 4, 5, 6, 7.

    • Formula A: $1 \cdot 4$ to $(2) \cdot 4 - 1 \Rightarrow 4 \text{ to } 7$. (Correct)

  • Block 2 ($k=2$): Contains words 8, 9, 10, 11.

    • Formula A: $2 \cdot 4$ to $(3) \cdot 4 - 1 \Rightarrow 8 \text{ to } 11$. (Correct)

 

Why other options are wrong:

 

  • B: Uses $p^2$, which would imply the block size grows quadratically, which is incorrect.

  • C: Uses $2^p$. This would be correct only if $p$ was defined as the number of offset bits (meaning block size is $2^p$). But the problem explicitly states the block size is $p$ words.

  • D: Also uses $2^p$, making it incorrect for the same reason as C.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Block numbers start from $0$.

Analogy to $0$-indexing in an Array:

  • $0^{\text{th}}$ has $0$ elements before it

  • $1^{\text{st}}$ has $1$ element before it

  • $2^{\text{nd}}$ has $2$ elements before it

  • $\vdots$

  • $i^{\text{th}}$ has $i$ elements before it

Similarly, in this question:

  • $k^{\text{th}}$ block has $k$ blocks before it $\implies k \cdot p$ words before it

  • $(k+1)^{\text{th}}$ block has $k+1$ blocks before it $\implies (k+1) \cdot p$ words before it

Thus, the range of words in the $k^{\text{th}}$ block is:

$$k \cdot p \text{ to } (k+1) \cdot p - 1$$

Answer: (A)

questions.html:
Consider a small two-way set-associative cache memory, consisting of four blocks. For choosing the block to be replaced, use the least recently used (LRU) scheme. The number of cache misses for the following sequence of block addresses is:

$$8, 12, 0, 12, 8$$
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/nUPpGN3nd5Y

$8$ - Compulsory/Cold Miss

$12$ - Compulsory/Cold Miss

$0$ - Compulsory/Cold Miss

$12$ - Hit

$8$ - Conflict Miss

We have $4$ blocks and $2$ blocks in a set

$\implies$ there are $2$ sets. So blocks will go to sets as follows:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf {Set Number} &  \textbf{Block Number} \\\hline \text{0} & \text{0,8,12}  \\\hline\text{1} &  \\\hline \end{array}$$
Since the lowest bit of block address is used for indexing into the set, so $8, 12$ and $0$ first miss in cache with $0$ replacing $8$ (there are two slots in each set due to $2-\text{way}$ set) and then $12$ hits in cache and $8$ again misses. So, totally $4$ misses.

Correct Answer: $C$

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/nUPpGN3nd5Y

questions.html: A $4$-way set-associative cache memory unit with a capacity of $16$ KB is built using a block size of $8$ words. The word length is $32$ bits. The size of the physical address space is $4$ GB. The number of bits for the TAG field is ____
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo 

Method 2 (Discussed in DVRUO Classes Cache Memory Lectures):

Number of sets$=\dfrac{\text{cache size}}{\text{size of a set}}$

Size of a set $=\text{block size}\times  \text{no. of blocks in a set}$

$= 8 \text{ words}\times 4\text{ (4-way set-associative)}$

$= 8\times 4\times 4\text{ (since a word is 32 bits = 4 bytes)}$

$= 128\text{ bytes}.$

So, number of sets $=\dfrac{16\ KB}{(128\ B)}=128$

Number of blocks in main memory = $4GB/32B = 2^{27}$

Now, we can divide the physical address space (i.e. main memory blocks) equally among these $128$ sets.

So, the number of main memory blocks that may possibly map to any particular set:

$=\dfrac{2^{27}}{128}$

$=2^{20}$

So, we need $20$ tag bits to identify one of these $2^{20}$ blocks.

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo
